definition.explanation.exceptions: Members of the role that the rule does not describe. These are the ones a committee reviews one by one.
definition.explanation.over_granting: People the rule would designate although they do not hold the role today. This is the security cost of simplification.
definition.explanation.power: How many times better the rule identifies members than a random draw. At 1 it teaches nothing: on a large repository, a tiny regularity can be statistically certain and worthless.
definition.explanation.reliability: Among the people the rule designates, the share that actually holds the role. What is missing to reach 100 % is the over-granting you would accept by applying the rule as it stands.
definition.explanation.rule: What the members of this role have in common, expressed over the attributes of your identity files. This is the sentence an application owner must be able to defend or challenge.
definition.key_policy.duplicate_key: Several rows carrying the same identifier. Discarding every occurrence loses the identifier but invents nothing; keeping the last is what an extract whose most recent row sits at the bottom calls for. The entitlements key is the (user, right) pair.
definition.key_policy.empty_key: A row whose identifier is not filled in designates nobody. Only two outcomes: refuse the load, or discard the row — « keep the first » would mean nothing for a key that designates nothing.
definition.mining.arbitrage: Weight of over-granting against coverage. This number is not typed in: the trade-off points derive it from the model you pick.
definition.mining.couverture_visee: Share of the existing entitlements the model must explain before it stops. Without a target, the product keeps every role that brings something — and the trade-off between coverage and over-granting then has no effect, since it only changes the order.
definition.mining.depth: Number of attributes crossed at once. This is the expensive parameter: the number of groups grows as the product of the cardinalities. A crossing is kept only if it explains what no single attribute explains.
definition.mining.inclure_sans_droit: Some identities in the repository hold no rights at all. With no status and no creation date, nothing tells a joiner — who will indeed receive the roles — from a leaver whose access was revoked. Unticked, the analysis ignores them: roles are built on the identities that hold something, and the reported over-granting does not count what those roles would give them. Ticked, they enter the computation: group coverage rates drop, so fewer roles are produced, but the reported cost is that of a real assignment. Either way the screen states how many rightless identities the proposed roles would reach.
definition.mining.min_coverage: Share of the group that must hold a right for it to enter the role. At 100 %, the role holds only what everybody has: few rights, no surprise. Lower, it holds what the majority has: richer, but granting it gives rights to the minority who did not have them.
definition.mining.min_rights: Number of rights below which a role is not proposed. A one-right role is not wrong, but it saves no decision: you may as well grant the right.
definition.mining.min_users: Headcount below which a group forms no role. Too low and you manufacture roles for three people that nobody will maintain; too high and you lose the small teams that do share a job.
definition.mining.over_granted_if_applie: Number of (identity, right) pairs the model would create the day it is actually assigned, each counted once. It adds to the computed over-granting whatever the roles would give the rightless identities their rule designates. Equal to the over-granting shown when those identities are counted; higher otherwise, and the gap measures what the computed figure leaves unsaid.
definition.mining.parcimonie: The engine may propose « role = nurse » and, next to it, « role = nurse AND ward = cardiology ». The second sometimes adds only a handful of rows. Measured on the bench, the engine keeps eleven times more of these sub-roles than actually exist. Parsimony requires a sub-role to beat its parent by a margin: at 3 %, useless sub-roles disappear without losing a real rule; beyond 5 %, real rules start to fall. It is not free — those sub-roles carry 43 % of the model's marginal coverage.
definition.mining.population_detail: An HR rule designates its members by a conjunction of criteria. Some of those members hold no rights today: the day the model is assigned, they receive the whole role. A rule's cost is the number of (identity, right) pairs that would create, each counted once. A high share — most of a group holding nothing — usually signals a population with no IT access at all, or an incomplete load: either way, a question to ask before deciding.
definition.nav.applications: The applications the rights belong to.
definition.nav.identities: The people in the repository, with their attributes. Kovex presupposes none of them: they are the columns of your files.
definition.nav.rights: The elementary authorisations inside an application: security group, profile, entitlement.
definition.perimeter.excluded: A by-name exclusion freezes an identifier: it suits the exception — that specific service account, that contractor — not a population, which is filtered by a rule. The difference matters on reload: a rule re-evaluates, a list does not, and identities that arrived since the decision escape the list unnoticed.
definition.perimeter.missing: On a real repository the column is incomplete. This choice decides the fate of identities where it is empty, and it is mandatory: deciding for you would settle the fate of a population you have not looked at.
definition.perimeter.rules: Rules decide who enters the analysis. They combine: an identity stays in scope if it satisfies every rule. A rule bears on an identity column and on the values it takes in the loaded repository — the product presumes no column. Dropping identities changes the denominator of every figure shown, so the analysed population is restated everywhere. A rule whose column has vanished from the repository drops nobody, and the screen says so.
definition.stats.apps_covered: Number of distinct applications those rights belong to.
definition.stats.avg_coverage: Average coverage of the proposed roles: for one role, the share of its rule's rights its members already hold.
definition.stats.compression: How many entitlements one link of the model grants on average. At 3.0, one link is worth three; below 1.0, the model costs more links than it grants entitlements.
definition.stats.habs_coverage: Share of real entitlements the roles explain. Coverage of 100 % with one role per person would be trivial and worthless.
definition.stats.over_granted: Rights the roles would grant to people who do not hold them today. This is the security cost of the simplification: raising coverage raises it too.
definition.stats.over_granted_share: Entitlements the model would create, as a share of those that exist today — the same denominator as coverage, so the two figures compare. Showing coverage without it tells only half the trade-off.
definition.stats.redundancy: Share of identity-right pairs covered by several roles at once. When high, it points to candidates that repeat one another.
definition.stats.rights_covered: Number of distinct rights carried by at least one candidate role.
definition.stats.roles_discovered: Number of candidate roles the analysis produced. A candidate is not a role: it becomes one when you approve it.
definition.stats.roles_found: Number of candidate business roles — the granting rules proposed from identity attributes.
definition.stats.total_users: Number of distinct identities at least one business role would cover.
definition.stats.uncovered: Real assignments that no proposed role explains. It is the counterpart of a model that grants nothing in excess: those assignments stay individual, and the figure is there to be decided rather than endured.
definition.stats.users_impacted: Number of identities at least one candidate role would cover. The rest would stay on individual grants.
definition.stats.wsc: Weight of the model: the number of roles plus the number of links it creates. A model nobody can read through has no operational value, whatever its coverage.
definition.stats.wsc_hierarchique: The same weight, counted as an IGA would hold it with inheritance: each role keeps only its own rights, each person is attached only to the widest role they hold, and each inheritance link counts as one. This is the structural complexity (WSC) of role mining publications.
definition.transformations.column: The column name as it appears in your file, not the standardised name: transformations apply before columns are mapped.
definition.transformations.order: Rules apply from top to bottom. Order matters: splitting a multi-valued cell then trimming each piece is not the same as the reverse.
